title: Gardening & Growing
strapline: From a seed in a small fist to something you can actually eat — the slowest, best magic we do.
intent: Children experience the full arc: sow a seed, tend it, watch it change, harvest it, taste it — and can tell the story afterwards.
Children learn that living things have needs — water, light, soil, time — and that meeting those needs is a responsibility, not a one-off job.
Children develop gentleness towards every living thing they meet in the soil: worms, woodlice, ladybirds, roots.
Children notice seasons and weather as things that matter — what the rain does for the beds, why nothing much happens in January.
Children use real tools for real work: trowels, watering cans, rakes and scissors at harvest.
Children grow the language of growing: seed, shoot, root, bud, ripe, wilt, compost.
implementation: Grow at least one fast win (cress, radishes, sunflowers) alongside one long game (potatoes, strawberries, pumpkins) — quick feedback and delayed reward both matter.
Make care a routine with real ownership: a watering rota with photo cards, children checking the beds at the same point each day.
Model gentle hands with every worm you meet — lift it, wonder at it, return it — and expect the same from everyone.
Narrate the invisible: 'the roots are drinking underground', 'this seed is still sleeping' — the interesting part is the part you can't see.
Measure and record together: photograph the same bed weekly, mark sunflower heights on a cane, count the tomatoes as they redden.
Let children do the real jobs with real tools — digging, filling cans at the butt, carrying, snipping herbs — supervised, not simulated.
Cook or eat what you grow within sight of where it grew, and send seeds or seedlings home to keep the growing going.
key_questions: What do you think this seed needs to start growing?
What's changed since we last looked?
What do you think is happening under the soil?
How will we know when it's ready to pick?
Where should we put the worm you found — and why there?

impact.text: Children water and check the beds with reminders, using gentle hands with everything alive they find.
Children link weather and seasons to the garden — 'the rain watered them for us', 'it's too cold for seeds now'.
Older children plant, tend and harvest as a responsibility they hold, not a job they're given.
Children talk about growth and change over time — comparing this week's photo to last week's, spotting the first shoot.
Children handle worms and minibeasts gently as a matter of course, and pull up a friend who doesn't.
Children can tell you the story of something they grew, from seed packet to plate.
Children use trowels, watering cans and harvest scissors with purpose and control.
Children compare and measure the garden — whose sunflower is taller, which pot has more, how many strawberries are ripe today.

enhancements: A see-through rootviewer — beans against the glass of a jar so the secret half of the plant is on show.
A wormery built with the children, fed with snack scraps and studied with magnifiers.
Sunflower race canes, one per child, with names and weekly height marks.
A potato bucket per key group with a ceremonial tipping-out harvest day.
Herb snipping station — scissors, rosemary and mint, and pots to fill for the mud kitchen.
A rain gauge and simple weather chart by the beds, checked on garden days.
Seed-saving envelopes in autumn: collect, label, store, and sow your own saved seeds in spring.

playing_exploring: Soil, water, seeds and creatures pull every sense into play — the garden is irresistible first, educational second.
Children make their own discoveries at their own pace: the worm under the pot, the first bent shoot.
active_learning: Growing rewards patience like nothing else — children wait weeks and find it worth it.
Daily care routines build the habit of seeing a responsibility through.
creating_thinking: Children predict, check and revise — 'I think it needs more water' is a hypothesis with a testable result.
They link causes to effects across time: sun, rain, growth, wilt, harvest.
